question: For affine sequence models whose input-dependent generators have a controlled Lie-algebraic structure, what exact-simulation obstruction is imposed by order-symmetric layers, how does stacking layers change the reachable Lie algebra and the local approximation error, and do symbolic and continuous state-tracking experiments distinguish representational depth benefits from finite-precision learnability?

key_findings.claim: The theory studies a regular, minimal, real-analytic affine-SSM abstraction; it does not directly classify every implemented Transformer, Mamba, GLA, or neural-network block.
key_findings.evidence: A model is defined by F_x(h)=A(x)h+b(x) on a finite-dimensional Euclidean state space with real-analytic A and b, locally bounded integrable input paths, and standard control-theoretic regularity and minimality. Its class is assigned from Lie({A(x)}), and a model is called restricted when that generator algebra is abelian even though the translation b(x) can remain order-sensitive. Implemented attention and diagonal SSMs are later treated as discretized or order-symmetric representatives, but no equivalence theorem maps their full nonlinear blocks, normalization, residual paths, finite precision, or positional encodings to the abstract class.

anchors.section: 2.2 State-space models and the Lie equation / Definitions 2.1-2.4
B.1-B.3 Abstract control systems, simulation, and minimality

key_findings.claim: A single restricted layer has an unavoidable order-sensitive mismatch on at least one constructed short input path, with the leading lower-bound scale set by the target system's second Magnus term.
key_findings.evidence: Lemma 3.1 rules out exact simulation of a general SSM by an abelian SSM. Theorem 3.2 strengthens this to approximation: compare a path with an admissible order permutation, use the restricted model's order symmetry, and lower-bound one target-state mismatch by a constant times the commutator mass ||Omega_2||. For affine restricted models, the appendix uses two controllability prefixes and four suffix-order inputs to cancel translation effects. The result is existential, local, and conditional on admissible reversed/permuted paths and minimality; it is not a uniform error formula for arbitrary data.

anchors.section: 3.1 Expressivity bounds of a single layer / Lemma 3.1 and Theorem 3.2
C.1-C.2 Proofs of Lemma 3.1 and Theorem 3.2

key_findings.claim: Depth supplies a solvable-algebra hierarchy: k abelian layers generate a Lie algebra of derived length at most k, while k restricted affine layers have derived length at most 2k.
key_findings.evidence: Proposition 3.3 constructs a nested chain of layer-supported ideals; Lie brackets remove the lowest active layer, so successive derived algebras move upward through the stack. This proves an upper class bound. It does not prove that every restricted k-layer architecture reaches derived length 2k or that 2k is necessary; the paper explicitly leaves the stronger necessity statement as Conjecture 3.9.

key_findings.claim: A Lie-algebra extension can be factored into a two-layer lifted SSM, and a solvable target of derived length k therefore admits an exact k-layer abelian realization with a smooth readout.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 3.4 locally factors the lifted group flow G(t) into a quotient trajectory H(t) and an ideal trajectory a(t) using a smooth local section of 1->A->G->H->1; vectorizing the matrix flow maps it back to an SSM. Iterating over the derived-series tower gives Corollary 3.5. The construction is local near the identity, allows a smooth output map, and can expand an n by n flow to n^2 state coordinates, so it is an existence result rather than a parameter- or hardware-efficient neural implementation.

anchors.section: C.4-C.5 Lift factorization, vectorization, and derived-series iteration

key_findings.claim: For a non-solvable target, the paper constructs a short-horizon abelian k-layer approximation whose leading Magnus-truncation error is O(epsilon^(2^k)), but this does not establish a global trained-model error law.
key_findings.evidence: With epsilon=int_0^T ||A(x(t))||dt<1, Corollary 3.6 quotients higher-order brackets to a nilpotent algebra. A class-(2^k-1) nilpotent algebra has derived length at most k, so k abelian layers preserve Magnus terms below order 2^k and the first discarded term is O(epsilon^(2^k)). The PDF was checked because text extraction flattens superscripts; arXiv v2 explicitly corrected this indexing. Big-O constants, state dimension, approximation-map complexity, and their dependence on k are not bounded. The long-horizon discussion invokes composition and says inputs can accumulate local error, but supplies no uniform global decay bound after repeated multiplication.

anchors.section: B.4 Magnus series and path signature

key_findings.claim: Any finite word problem of length at most T has a constructive abelian realization with at most floor(log2 T)+1 layers, but its worst-case width grows as O(n^T/T) for an alphabet of size n.
key_findings.evidence: Proposition 3.7 uses Chen-Fox-Lyndon factorization, a free Lie algebra indexed by Lyndon words, and truncation after word length T. The resulting class-T nilpotent algebra has derived length at most floor(log2 T)+1 and is converted to an abelian stack. Corollary 3.8 applies Witt's formula to show exponential total state dimension. Thus logarithmic depth is bought with exponential width and a smooth readout, and applies only to bounded-length sequences rather than arbitrary-length exact state tracking.

anchors.section: C.7-C.8 Completion and Witt dimension formula

key_findings.claim: On length-256 solvable word problems, transition structure matters at least as much as nominal depth: a one-layer DeltaProduct solves every reported task, whereas deeper diagonal models often remain at zero sequence accuracy.
key_findings.evidence: Models train on length 128 and test on 256. Table 2 reports DeltaProduct at 1.00 sequence-level accuracy on C2, C3, D8, H3, S3, and S4 with one layer. Signed Mamba scores 1.00 on C2 at one layer and, at two layers, 1.00 on C2, D8, and H3 plus 0.19 on S3, but 0 on C3 and S4. AUSSM reaches 1.00 on only C2 and C3 at both depths and 0 on all four non-abelian tasks. Transformer, positive-only Mamba, and one- or two-layer positive GLA are 0 throughout. These results support a learnability/inductive-bias gap, not a monotone empirical depth law.

anchors.section: Table 2 and 4.1 Length generalization on solvable word problems
4.1 Abelian, nilpotent, and solvable word problems

key_findings.claim: The word-problem table is an optimistic best-of-search result with no independent uncertainty estimate, and the stated protocol appears to monitor the same length-generalization split used for reporting.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix D.1 searches 3 hidden sizes, 4 learning rates, and 2 batch sizes, runs each configuration with 3 seeds for 100 epochs, reports the best results, and says it monitors length-generalization performance and stops early at 100% sequence accuracy. Training uses 500,000 sequences except C2 at 100,000, while evaluation uses 1,000 length-256 sequences. No separate validation split, selection rule across seeds, confidence interval, or all-seed distribution is reported, so the exact 0/1 table cannot be read as an unbiased population estimate.

key_findings.claim: Depth raises the maximum A5 sequence length attaining the plotted threshold, but Figure 2 uses training accuracy and omits deeper points that fail to beat shallower models.
key_findings.evidence: For the non-solvable A5 word problem, Figure 2 plots the maximum sequence length with greater than 90% training sequence accuracy. Transformer improves from one through eight layers roughly along the logarithmic-depth reference, while GLA and Signed Mamba improve only through about four or five layers. Six- and seven-layer Signed Mamba do not beat five layers and are omitted; eight layers reaches length 36 versus 35 at five layers. Because the caption says training accuracy, all models were trained on lengths up to 128, and underperforming deep points are suppressed, the plot is a capacity/trainability diagnostic rather than a length-generalization or error-bound validation.

anchors.section: 4.2 Depth vs. length in non-solvable word problems / Figure 2

key_findings.claim: A continuous A5 rigid-rotation task shows qualitatively lower mean-squared error with depth, but gains saturate for the diagonal SSMs and do not test the predicted O(epsilon^(2^k)) dependence.
key_findings.evidence: Two rotations of 120 and 72 degrees generate the dodecahedral A5 action in SO(3), and models predict a unit vector after each action. Across train lengths to 128 and test lengths to 256, Figure 3 shows lower MSE for deeper Transformer, GLA, and Signed Mamba models with standard error over three seeds. GLA and Signed Mamba saturate beyond six layers; deep Transformers show seed variability; a one-layer DeltaProduct with four Householder products remains near zero. No commutator mass, epsilon, fit slope, or depth-dependent Big-O constant is measured.

anchors.section: D.2 A5-rotated vector prediction task / hyperparameters

key_findings.claim: AUSSM supplies a clear negative result: formal complex/unitary capacity does not translate into learned non-abelian tracking in this setup.
key_findings.evidence: AUSSM solves the two abelian tests but is 0 on D8, H3, S3, and S4 with either one or two layers. On the rotation regression it is unstable and subpar and is moved to Appendix Figure 4. The implementation disables mixed precision for complex values and has sequence-length constraints. This is consistent with the paper's expressivity-versus-learnability distinction and contradicts any reading that richer eigenvalues plus nominal depth suffice operationally.

anchors.section: D.1 AUSSM implementation and model class

key_findings.claim: The experiments validate a qualitative depth benefit on selected state-tracking tasks, not the paper's quantitative approximation theorem or an exponential empirical scaling law.
key_findings.evidence: The symbolic studies report sequence-level success thresholds, while the rotation study reports MSE curves under a fixed training recipe. Neither constructs target/model pairs with known epsilon and Omega_2, evaluates the theorem's infimum over projection maps, measures Magnus truncation terms, controls width according to the construction, or compares observed error with epsilon^(2^k). Saturation, omitted deep points, and instability are prominent. The theoretical and empirical portions are directionally consistent but not a direct theorem test.

key_findings.claim: Finite precision and optimization are unresolved bridges between the real-arithmetic constructions and the measured architectures.
key_findings.evidence: The authors explicitly state that the theory uses real arithmetic, whereas empirical computation is finite precision; exponentially small errors may fall below numerical resolution, and finite precision may obstruct optimization. The experiments also show deeper models underperforming or becoming unstable. Current finite-precision competitors obtain architecture-specific exact characterizations that do not automatically follow from this smooth-control construction.

key_findings.claim: After direct comparison, the defensible novelty is the continuous-time Lie-extension and local Magnus-error synthesis, not the broad facts that constant-depth parallel models have state-tracking limits or that logarithmic depth can simulate bounded automata.
key_findings.evidence: Earlier work gives TC0 limitations for common SSMs, O(log T)-depth Transformer automaton simulation, finite-precision if-and-only-if depth characterizations for complex diagonal SSMs on solvable groups, and one-layer structured-transition models that solve A5. This paper uniquely combines affine controlled Lie equations, commutator-mass lower bounds, extension-tower factorization, and an O(epsilon^(2^k)) local construction. Its overlap with the concurrent ICLR 2026 diagonal-SSM result is substantial on the depth/solvability and empirical learnability conclusions.

method.core_idea: Lift affine state evolution to a controlled Lie equation, use commutators to measure the order information destroyed by restricted parallelizable layers, then relate network depth to successive Lie-algebra extensions and approximate non-solvable flows by truncating their Magnus expansion.
method.mechanism: The input-dependent generator family A(x) defines a Lie algebra. A path and its reordered counterpart expose the second Magnus commutator term that an abelian generator cannot reproduce. A short exact sequence 0->a->g->h->0 locally factors the lifted group trajectory into quotient and ideal flows, which become two stacked SSM layers; iterating a solvable derived series yields abelian layers. For non-solvable targets, quotienting high lower-central-series terms preserves Magnus terms through order 2^k-1, giving leading local error O(epsilon^(2^k)). A separate free-Lie/Lyndon-word construction gives logarithmic depth for bounded word problems, with exponential state width.
assumptions: The target and approximating systems are finite-dimensional affine SSMs on Euclidean state spaces.
Generator and translation maps are real analytic, with the regularity needed for controlled ODE existence and local Lie integration.
Systems satisfy the control-theoretic minimality or controllability/observability conditions used to turn flow mismatch into state or output mismatch.
Reordered or time-reversed comparison paths remain admissible inputs.
The time window is small enough for the Magnus series and local group-section constructions to converge.
The local generator mass epsilon is below one.
A smooth output map and state augmentation/vectorization are permitted in simulation.
Worst-case state dimension and readout complexity are not constrained when proving depth sufficiency.
Piecewise-constant continuous inputs faithfully represent discrete word symbols.
Real-arithmetic exact constructions are informative about finite-precision trained models.
Implemented attention and structured-SSM blocks retain the relevant order-symmetry or generator-algebra restriction despite their additional nonlinear components.
A model's algebraic expressivity class is separable from whether gradient descent can discover the realizing parameters.
Best-of-grid symbolic experiments and three-seed rotation curves are sufficient qualitative diagnostics of the theory.
Local approximation orders remain meaningful when short flows are composed over long horizons, despite absent global stability constants.

techniques.role: Replaces a single hidden-state trajectory with its state-transition flow so the generator Lie algebra can classify order sensitivity.
Uses the norm of the second Magnus term as a leading measure of the target dynamics lost under input-order symmetry.
Compares an input path with a reordered or reversed path to force at least one restricted-model state mismatch.
Decomposes an extension flow into quotient and ideal trajectories realized as two stacked SSM layers.
Maps successive abelian extension factors to layer count and bounds the solvable class of a finite stack.
Quotients high-order commutators so k abelian layers match progressively higher Magnus orders.
Memorizes all bounded-length order interactions in a truncated free Lie algebra to obtain logarithmic depth.
Uses Witt's formula to expose the exponential state-dimension cost hidden behind the logarithmic-depth construction.
Tests abelian, nilpotent, solvable, and non-solvable order structures with known group classes.
Embeds the non-solvable A5 action in SO(3) to test depth on continuous-valued state tracking.

evaluations.setting: C2, C3, D8, H3, S3, and S4 prefix-product word problems; training length 128 and test length 256 with sequence-level exact accuracy.
evaluations.metric: Fraction of 1,000 test sequences for which every prefix label is correct.
evaluations.result: One-layer DeltaProduct scores 1.00 on all six tasks. Two-layer Signed Mamba scores 1.00 on C2, D8, and H3, 0.19 on S3, and 0 on C3 and S4. One- and two-layer AUSSM score 1.00 only on C2 and C3. Transformer, positive Mamba, and positive GLA variants report 0 throughout.
evaluations.baseline: Transformer, positive-only Mamba/GLA, Signed Mamba, AUSSM, and a general-transition DeltaProduct reference.

evaluations.setting: The same word problems with 24 hyperparameter combinations from hidden size, learning rate, and batch size, each run with three random seeds for up to 100 epochs.
evaluations.metric: Best monitored length-generalization sequence accuracy, with early stopping at 100%.
evaluations.result: The paper reports only the selected best table entry, not mean or dispersion across configurations/seeds; the protocol says length-generalization performance is monitored and does not identify a separate selection split.
evaluations.baseline: No unselected-grid or held-out-selection result is supplied.

evaluations.setting: Non-solvable A5 word problem, models of depth 1-8, trained on sequence lengths up to 128.
evaluations.metric: Maximum sequence length attaining greater than 90% training sequence accuracy.
evaluations.result: Transformer improves across depth roughly with the logarithmic reference; GLA and Signed Mamba improve through about depth 4-5 and then saturate. Signed Mamba reaches length 35 at five layers and 36 at eight; six- and seven-layer points that do not improve are omitted.
evaluations.baseline: The theoretical floor(log2 T)+1 upper-bound curve and DeltaProduct.

evaluations.setting: Continuous unit-vector prediction under sequences of 120-degree and 72-degree rotations generating A5; train lengths through 128, test lengths through 256, three seeds.
evaluations.metric: Mean-squared vector prediction error versus sequence length with standard error.
evaluations.result: Increasing depth generally lowers error for Transformer, GLA, and Signed Mamba, but GLA/Signed Mamba gains saturate beyond roughly six layers and deep Transformer has high variability. DeltaProduct with four Householder products is near zero.
evaluations.baseline: One-layer DeltaProduct with four Householder products and shallower versions of each architecture.

evaluations.setting: The same A5 rotation task with AUSSM at depths 1-8.
evaluations.metric: Train/test mean-squared error versus sequence length over three seeds.
evaluations.result: AUSSM is unstable and generally subpar; the authors move the result to Appendix Figure 4 and attribute it provisionally to complex-model trainability.
evaluations.baseline: DeltaProduct and the Transformer/GLA/Signed-Mamba curves in the main figure.

limitations: Author-stated: the work analyzes expressivity and approximation rather than learnability, optimization, or architecture-specific inductive bias.
Author-stated: the exact algebraic class of a real-world task is rarely known, limiting direct model-selection use.
Author-stated: large-scale language-model and multimodal experiments are outside scope.
Author-stated: the real-arithmetic theory may interact nontrivially with finite numerical precision.
Author-stated: positional encodings, especially multiplicative variants, may change expressivity and are not covered.
Author-stated: deep models are difficult to train in the experiments, with saturation, instability, and occasional regression.
Reviewer-identified: Theorems 3.2 and 3.4 rely on local windows, admissible path permutations, minimality, and local smooth sections; broad global statements need additional stability conditions.
Reviewer-identified: Corollary 3.6 is an existence upper order O(epsilon^(2^k)), not a lower bound, fitted empirical law, or uniform long-horizon guarantee.
Reviewer-identified: constants, state width, output-map complexity, conditioning, and their dependence on depth are not bounded in the approximation claim.
Reviewer-identified: the exact realization allows smooth readouts and vectorized lifted flows, so it does not automatically produce a standard efficient Transformer or diagonal-SSM block.
Reviewer-identified: Proposition 3.3 supplies upper derived-length bounds; the corresponding necessity result for restricted stacks remains a conjecture.
Reviewer-identified: the logarithmic-depth word construction has exponential O(n^T/T) width and only bounded-length validity.
Reviewer-identified: Table 2 selects the best of a 24-configuration by three-seed search and reports no uncertainty.
Reviewer-identified: Appendix D says length-generalization performance is monitored, but no independent validation split is described before reporting the length-256 test result.
Reviewer-identified: Figure 2 uses training, not held-out, accuracy and hides deep configurations that fail to exceed shallower maximum lengths.
Reviewer-identified: no experiment measures epsilon, Omega_2, Magnus orders, or the theorem's projection-map approximation error.
Reviewer-identified: empirical tasks are small finite groups and one A5 rotation system, with no natural language, code, MDP, noisy, partially observed, or unknown-algebra task.
Reviewer-identified: zero sequence-level accuracy can hide useful token-level or shorter-prefix behavior because one error makes the entire sequence incorrect.
failure_modes: A task with non-solvable order structure cannot be exactly represented by any fixed-depth restricted stack under the paper's abstraction.
A locally accurate Magnus truncation can become inaccurate under long composition if transition norms amplify rather than stably accumulate errors.
The theoretical realizing stack can be unusable because its width or smooth readout grows exponentially or is ill-conditioned.
Finite precision can erase the promised high-order improvement or make the constructed coordinates numerically unstable.
Gradient descent can fail to find an available non-abelian solution, as AUSSM and deeper diagonal models demonstrate.
A model can have the correct nominal algebraic capacity yet choose a brittle fixed-length shortcut that fails beyond training length.
A positional encoding, residual path, gating nonlinearity, or normalization layer can invalidate the simple generator-algebra classification.
Best-of-grid selection on the evaluation regime can make an architecture appear to solve a task without reproducible seed-level reliability.
Sequence-level exact accuracy can collapse to zero from sparse prefix errors and obscure partial competence.
Deeper models can underperform through optimization instability; omitted points in a monotone-depth plot can conceal this.
A restricted model may approximate a low-commutator regime well but fail abruptly when inputs traverse higher-curvature or longer-horizon regions.
A smooth output map can perform much of the computation, making a nominal layer-count comparison misleading without readout constraints.
reusable_insights: Separate exact algebraic capacity, local approximation order, finite-precision implementation, and gradient-based learnability; they are four distinct claims.
Use a path and an order-permuted counterpart to isolate irreducible order-sensitive error while holding input content fixed.
Magnus terms provide a graded diagnostic: measure which nested commutator orders a sequence architecture preserves rather than only whether it exactly solves a task.
Report both layer depth and the state/readout width required by a constructive simulation; logarithmic depth alone can hide exponential resources.
Include a structured non-diagonal one-layer control such as DeltaProduct to determine whether depth is compensating for a transition restriction.
Evaluate the predicted approximation variable directly by controlling generator mass and measuring commutator terms across depth.
Use independent validation for hyperparameter/seed selection and retain every depth point, including regressions.
Pair sequence-level exact accuracy with prefix/token error and length-extrapolation curves to reveal partial and brittle solutions.
Test algebraic claims under both exact/high precision and deployment precision to distinguish structural obstruction from numerical failure.
When extending local bounds to long horizons, state and test the stability or contraction condition that controls error propagation.
open_questions: Can the O(epsilon^(2^k)) local construction be strengthened to a uniform long-horizon bound with explicit depth-dependent constants?
What matching lower bounds show when the exponent 2^k or the derived-length layer count is necessary rather than merely sufficient?
Can the extension construction be realized with polynomial width, simple readouts, and the exact transition restrictions used by efficient neural SSMs?
Does the conjectured derived-length limitation for restricted k-layer affine SSMs hold?
How do finite precision, quantization, and conditioning change the Magnus-truncation depth benefit?
Can training objectives or curricula reliably recover the solvable extension factors that the theory says exist?
Do measured commutator mass and higher Magnus terms predict real model error on code execution, entity tracking, or learned world models?
How do additive and multiplicative positional encodings alter the relevant Lie algebra and error order?
What happens for stochastic, partially observed, non-minimal, or nonsmooth physical systems outside the assumptions?
Would a preregistered all-seed comparison reproduce the reported architecture rankings and depth saturation?
Can adaptive depth allocate layers according to online estimates of local order sensitivity without losing parallel efficiency?

competitive_landscape.title: The Expressive Limits of Diagonal SSMs for State-Tracking
competitive_landscape.difference: Shakerinava et al. prove at finite precision that a k-layer input-dependent complex diagonal SSM tracks a group if and only if it has a length-k subnormal series with abelian factors, and they empirically expose the same solvable-task learnability gap. Heo et al. use smooth affine controlled Lie algebras, give broader extension constructions and a local O(epsilon^(2^k)) approximation result outside the exact class, but their restricted-stack necessity is only conjectured. The overlap narrows novelty to the Lie-control and graded-error synthesis.

competitive_landscape.title: The Illusion of State in State-Space Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Merrill et al. place common log-precision S4/S6-style models in uniform TC0 and derive failures on NC1-hard state tracking such as permutation composition, with Mamba experiments. Heo et al. replace the complexity-class obstruction with a geometric commutator measure and ask how approximation changes with depth; they do not strengthen the finite-precision complexity lower bound.

competitive_landscape.title: Transformers Learn Shortcuts to Automata
competitive_landscape.difference: Liu et al. already construct polynomial-size O(log T)-depth Transformer simulators for arbitrary finite automata of length T via hierarchical/Krohn-Rhodes ideas and test brittleness. Heo et al.'s Proposition 3.7 obtains a similar logarithmic layer upper bound for abelian SSMs via truncated free Lie algebras and makes its exponential worst-case width explicit, while adding continuous-state and local-error results.

competitive_landscape.title: Structured Linear CDEs: Maximally Expressive and Parallel-in-Time Sequence Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Walker et al. design block-diagonal, sparse, and Walsh-Hadamard input-dependent transitions that retain dense-matrix expressivity, solve A5 with one layer, and report strong regular-language length generalization plus about 20-fold faster training than log-NCDEs. Heo et al. analyze how restricted layers can approximate missing order structure through depth rather than proposing a one-layer maximally expressive efficient transition.

competitive_landscape.title: DeltaProduct: Improving State-Tracking in Linear RNNs via Householder Products
competitive_landscape.difference: DeltaProduct uses products of n_h generalized Householder transformations, giving diagonal-plus-rank-n_h transitions with a finite-precision expressivity/efficiency knob and gains on state tracking, length extrapolation, and language modeling. It is the one-layer perfect reference in Heo et al.'s solvable table and near-zero A5 rotation baseline; the new paper explains restricted-depth compensation but does not beat this general-transition control.

competitive_landscape.title: Unlocking State-Tracking in Linear RNNs Through Negative Eigenvalues
competitive_landscape.relationship: architecture-specific state-tracking precursor and baseline source
competitive_landscape.difference: Grazzi et al. prove positive-eigenvalue finite-precision LRNNs cannot solve parity, characterize additional structure needed for modular counting, and show negative-eigenvalue Mamba/DeltaNet improvements at model scale. Heo et al. use Signed Mamba to show that removing the simplest spectral obstruction solves C2 but still leaves major non-abelian learnability failures; their Lie brackets cover a broader kind of order sensitivity.

competitive_landscape.title: Bridging Expressivity and Scalability with Adaptive Unitary SSMs
competitive_landscape.relationship: complex/unitary restricted-SSM competitor and evaluated baseline
competitive_landscape.difference: Karuvally et al. introduce input-dependent skew-symmetric/unitary recurrence, prove logarithmic-precision simulation of solvable group automata, implement a parallel kernel, and report gains on modular arithmetic and time series. Heo et al. place complex diagonal behavior in their restricted hierarchy and find AUSSM fails every tested non-abelian word problem and is unstable on A5 rotation, emphasizing learnability rather than disputing formal capacity.

competitive_landscape.title: The Effect of Depth on the Expressivity of Deep Linear State-Space Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Bao et al. analyze deep linear time-invariant SSMs, showing unconstrained depth/width equivalences and advantages of depth under parameter-norm constraints, with constructive minimal-depth upper bounds and numerical tests. Heo et al. target input-dependent noncommutative order structure and local Magnus error instead, so the mechanisms differ, but the broad novelty phrase about depth and SSM expressivity should acknowledge this direct prior depth analysis.

competitive_landscape.title: Theoretical Foundations of Deep Selective State-Space Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Cirone et al. use rough-path signatures to show that selective random recurrences project nonlinear cross-token interactions at multiple time scales, providing an expressivity account for deep Mamba/GLA-like models. Heo et al. connect the closely related log-signature/Magnus view to explicit Lie-extension depth classes and an approximation order, but works under stronger regularity and does not study random-feature dimension or learning guarantees.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims a Lie-algebraic correspondence between sequence-model depth and towers of algebra extensions, an unavoidable commutator-mass error for restricted layers, and exponentially diminishing approximation error with depth, supported on symbolic word and continuous state-tracking tasks.
novelty_assessment.evidence: Theorems 3.2 and 3.4, Corollaries 3.5-3.6, and Propositions 3.7-3.8 form a coherent new continuous-control synthesis: a local commutator lower bound, exact extension factorization, O(epsilon^(2^k)) Magnus truncation order, and an explicit depth-width tradeoff. Experiments consistently show some benefit from depth but also strong transition-structure and learnability effects.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The Lie-extension plus graded local-error framework is a meaningful theoretical contribution. Claims should remain local, constructive, width-unconstrained, and separate from neural learnability. Constant-depth limitations, logarithmic bounded-automata simulation, solvable-group depth hierarchies, and one-layer A5-capable structured transitions substantially predate or closely coincide with this paper. The experiments do not verify exponential error decay; they provide only qualitative direction under optimistic model selection and small algebraic benchmarks.

reviewer_notes: All 28 extracted pages were read, including the Lie/control preliminaries, all theorem proofs, the affine restricted-model construction, Magnus and Lyndon-word appendices, hyperparameter protocol, AUSSM implementation notes, and both rotation figures. PDF pages 5-8 and 28 were directly inspected to resolve the corrected v2 exponent O(epsilon^(2^k)), Table 2 cells, the Figure 2 training-accuracy caption, omitted deep points, and plotted uncertainty. Author statements are reported as such; conclusions about locality, hidden resource costs, model-selection optimism, and absence of an empirical scaling-law test are reviewer inferences or contradiction audits. Nine current primary arXiv records were inspected on 2026-08-23 across mechanism/task, evaluation/baseline, and novelty/predecessor query families. This is a primary full-text pass, not secondary verification.
